implementation_notes: Python absorbs the pattern into a decorator: functools.cache is documented as a simple lightweight unbounded function cache, sometimes called memoize, and it is lru_cache(maxsize=None) - a dictionary lookup keyed by the arguments - so the classic dict-guard disappears entirely. Two documented properties drive the design: the cache is threadsafe (its structure stays coherent under concurrent updates) yet the wrapped function may still be called more than once if another thread misses the same key before the first call completes, and arguments must be hashable, so lists and dicts have to be canonicalised. The unbounded form is the right default for a fixed or small key domain and the wrong one for request-derived keys; there the bounded lru_cache variant is the honest choice.
pitfalls: Unbounded and never evicting: keyed by request data, the cache is a leak, because entries and their argument references stay until the process ends.
Decorating a method puts self in the key, so every instance - and everything it references - stays alive as long as the cache does.
Unhashable arguments raise TypeError; convert lists/dicts to tuples/frozensets or memoize on an explicit canonical key.
Concurrent misses may compute twice, and the cache keeps references to arguments and results (documented), so large objects are pinned by a hit.

variants.name: functools.lru_cache with a size bound
variants.implementation_notes: lru_cache(maxsize=N) is the same machinery with an eviction policy attached, and it is the documented answer for long-running processes: the size limit keeps the cache from growing without bound, cache_info() reports hits/misses/currsize for tuning N, cache_clear() invalidates everything, and typed=True separates arguments of different types. The docs also warn that distinct argument patterns are distinct calls - f(a=1, b=2) and f(b=2, a=1) are two entries - and that the object is best used only where previously computed values are genuinely reusable, not on functions with side effects, generators or clock/randomness-dependent results. It replaces the unbounded decorator exactly when the key domain is not bounded by construction.
pitfalls: Eviction is silent: after eviction the next call recomputes, so a too-small maxsize makes the function slower than no cache at all.
cache_clear() is all-or-nothing; there is no per-key invalidation in the standard library, so partial invalidation needs an explicit dict.
The cache keeps strong references to arguments and results (documented), so caching methods or big objects pins them.
Keyword order and default arguments create distinct cache entries, which can make a nominally identical call miss.

variants.name: cached_property for per-instance derived values
variants.implementation_notes: For an expensive attribute of an effectively immutable object, cached_property is the shape Python offers: the getter runs on first access and the value is then an ordinary attribute in the instance dictionary, so later reads bypass the descriptor. It replaces the classic self._x = None guard, and deletion (or __dict__.pop) is the documented way to make it recompute. Two documented limits make the choice explicit: since Python 3.12 it carries no lock, so the getter may run more than once under concurrent first access (guard it yourself if that matters), and it requires a mutable instance dictionary, so classes using __slots__ without __dict__ cannot use it.
pitfalls: No locking since 3.12: concurrent first access can run the getter more than once, and the last writer wins.
It requires a mutable __dict__, so it raises on classes that use __slots__ without one, and it interferes with PEP 412 key-sharing.
Assigning to the attribute shadows the descriptor forever, which silently disables recomputation.
It caches per instance for the instance's lifetime and never releases values tied to stale data; invalidation must be wired into every mutator.
